blocks.text: The phrase “new heavens and new earth” in verse 22 has been understood in different ways: as transformation, renewal, or replacement. Those possibilities remain debated. Later reflection on this language treats righteousness as central to the new reality, while Isaiah itself emphasizes the enduring place of God’s people and their worship.

Isaiah’s final vision joins judgment with restoration: nations and languages are gathered to see God’s glory, worship is pictured as extending to “all flesh,” and the new heavens and earth endure. Within Isaiah, related images of death’s defeat, bodily revival, renewed Jerusalem, and new creation became foundational for later Jewish and Christian hope concerning resurrection and new creation.

sections.title: The Scope of the Final Vision

blocks.text: The Great Isaiah Scroll is an almost complete copy of Isaiah’s sixty-six chapters. It broadly agrees with the Masoretic tradition while also containing many spelling and substantive differences; other Isaiah manuscripts and interpretive writings show that the book was actively copied and interpreted. This makes it important to distinguish a passage’s literary sense and historical referent from later uses such as typology, quotation, allusion, canonical synthesis, Jewish reception, or later Christian and ecclesial readings.
